UNIT 27: HUMANITARIAN ASSISTANCE

KEY THEME
- Ireland's humanitarian assistance programme gives immediate life-saving help (food, water, medical care) in short-term emergencies such as a crisis or disaster.
- Ireland's overseas development cooperation programme gives long-term sustainable aid to help countries support themselves over time.

LEARNING OUTCOME 3.1
- Explain the Irish government's approach to humanitarian assistance and its overseas development cooperation programmes.
- Describe humanitarian assistance in response to the war in Sudan.
- Discuss the role and activities of Irish Aid in Ethiopia.

KEY TERMS
- Humanitarian assistance: giving urgent help to people in need during emergencies such as wars, earthquakes or floods. It provides essentials like food, water, shelter and first aid, as quickly and fairly as possible, to all people regardless of political or religious background.
- Humanitarian aid: short-term help given to people in need during a crisis or emergency.
- Bilateral aid: financial assistance given to a developing country by a single donor country.
- Multilateral aid: financial assistance given to a developing country by an international organisation, e.g. the EU or UN.
- NGO (non-governmental organisation): a group that works to help others and solve problems but is not part of any government. Usually not-for-profit; often works on health, education or disaster relief.
- Civil war: a war between different groups within the same country, often over who should be in charge or how the country should be run.
- Ethnic cleansing: when a group forces people of a different race, religion or ethnicity to leave an area, often with threats or violence, so only one group remains.
- UNHCR: the UN Refugee Agency, which works so everyone has the right to seek asylum and find safe refuge after fleeing violence, persecution or war.
- Overseas Development Aid / Official Development Assistance (ODA): wealthy countries partnering with poorer nations to provide aid, funding and resources to improve living conditions.

IRELAND'S HUMANITARIAN ASSISTANCE: TWO RESPONSES
- Ireland responds to crises domestically (at home) and internationally (overseas).

DOMESTIC RESPONSE: THE HUMANITARIAN ASSISTANCE SCHEME
- A government programme to help people in Ireland whose homes are damaged by severe weather (storms, flooding) and who cannot afford the essential costs of recovery.
- It is NOT full compensation; it aims to reduce hardship and help families get back on their feet quickly.
- It gives money to people badly affected by disasters who cannot get help from insurance. Emergency costs like accommodation, heat and urgent needs are paid by local authorities.

CASE STUDY: STORM ÉOWYN (JANUARY 2025)
- Winds of more than 170 km/h and heavy rain.
- Thousands of homes lost electricity and water; many flooded or badly damaged (e.g. fallen trees and electricity wires; the Connacht GAA air dome was destroyed).
- Local community centres became Emergency Response Hubs giving hot food, water, battery charging, showers and basic medical care.
- Local authorities checked on vulnerable or isolated people so no one was left without help.
- Over €316,000 was paid out for 1,613 household claims within weeks of the storm.
- Community welfare officers nationwide helped families get support and find alternative accommodation.
- The scheme helped buy generators, gas heaters and torches when power cuts lasted days.

INTERNATIONAL RESPONSE
- Designed to help people in urgent need wherever a major disaster or crisis strikes (wars, natural disasters, famine).
- The Irish Aid programme works with trusted organisations like the UN, the Red Cross and local NGOs to get help quickly to those most in need.
- Help targets the most vulnerable groups: women, children and refugees, ensuring justice and fairness.
- Pre-positioning of emergency funds: Ireland gives money in advance to trusted groups like the UN. When disaster strikes the money can be accessed quickly, often within 72 hours, to buy and deliver food, clean water, shelter and medicines. Quick action in the first few days saves lives.
- Success lies in preparedness and being ready at short notice.

IRISH AID HUMANITARIAN SUPPORT 2023 (FIGURE 27.5)
- Supported 23 humanitarian partners including UN agencies, the Red Cross and NGOs.
- 72% of funding targeted forgotten and underfunded emergencies, including Syria, Yemen, the Sahel and the Horn of Africa.
- 385 tonnes of emergency stocks deployed to Turkey and Syria, South Sudan, Afghanistan and Gaza.
- 23 rapid response members deployed to UN agencies in 14 countries; 55 new experts added to the roster.
- Quick funding for earthquakes in Syria, Turkey and Morocco, flooding in Libya and the conflict in Gaza.
- Ireland is a Top 10 donor to the UN Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF). In 2023 Ireland was appointed to the CERF Advisory Group.
- At COP 28, Ireland was one of the first donors to announce funding (€5m) to CERF's new Climate Account.

CASE STUDY: SUDAN'S HUMANITARIAN DISASTER
The conflict
- April 2023: two rival military groups, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), plunged Sudan into a brutal civil war.
- Families forced to flee. Communities attacked for belonging to the 'wrong' group; ethnic cleansing forced people from their towns.
- Civilians are the main victims, targeted even when trying to reach hospitals or aid organisations. Aid workers have been attacked, making relief dangerous.
- The crisis spilled into neighbouring countries such as South Sudan and Chad: over 4 million refugees in overcrowded camps across the border, with too little food and diseases spreading rapidly.
- Described as the world's worst humanitarian crisis in recent years.
- By 2026 nearly two in three Sudanese needed help with food, water, shelter and safety, and up to 14 million people had left their homes. Famine has been declared in some regions.
Humanitarian zones map (Figure 27.8)
- Regions shaded by colour to show areas controlled by the rival groups or highly affected by violence (violent zones, high internal displacement, external displacement, border restrictions).
- Helps aid workers see where help is most urgent and which borders are less dangerous for escape.
- Moving between zones is risky: fighting, landmines, roadblocks, uncertain food and water.
- Map figures: 814,518 households displaced; 4,075,930 internally displaced persons (IDPs); 1,104,360 displaced to neighbouring countries. Of those leaving Sudan, Chad took 42.1%, Egypt 25.8%, South Sudan 22.9%, Ethiopia 7.2%, Central African Republic 1.6%, Libya 0.3%. Regions with the largest shares of IDPs include River Nile (12.24%), South Darfur (11.93%) and East Darfur (11.47%).
Ireland's response
- In 2024 the Irish government donated over €14 million for humanitarian aid in Sudan, plus €2.5 million for refugees in neighbouring countries.
- Ireland's embassy in Ethiopia gave targeted help to Sudanese refugees at the Ura refugee camp, focused on protection, water and sanitation for refugees and host communities.
- Funding went to Irish charities (GOAL, Trócaire, Concern) and global organisations (UN, Red Cross, World Health Organization) who make sure money and supplies go straight to those most in need (e.g. WHO emergency health kits).
- Over 50 tonnes of emergency supplies (airlifted) for Sudanese families who fled to South Sudan: tents, blankets, water cans, lamps, hygiene kits and mosquito nets, distributed in border camps.
- In West Darfur, Concern Worldwide organised truckloads of water cans, blankets and soap for thousands of families trapped by violence.
- Aid built shelters and gave food, clean water and medical care, protecting people from hunger and diseases such as cholera and typhoid.
- Irish support reached starving families in the Zamzam camp, North Darfur, treating malnutrition and saving lives, especially of children and mothers.
- It helps people still trapped in Sudan and those who escaped. Ireland remains committed for as long as needed.
Standing for peace
- Irish leaders speak at the UN General Assembly (193 member states, meets yearly in New York) demanding a ceasefire and better protection for civilians, highlighting the suffering of women and girls and pressing for humanitarian access.
- Difficulties of aid in conflict zones: attacks on aid workers and civilians, landmines, roadblocks, dangerous borders.

OVERSEAS DEVELOPMENT AID (ODA)
- Partnership between wealthy and poorer nations; projects deliver clean water, quality healthcare, nutritious food, education and training.
- Goal: stronger, healthier, more independent communities.
- Summary goals: reduce poverty, promote equality, respond to emergencies, support education and health, encourage peacebuilding.

IRISH AID
- Ireland's ODA programme. Aims for long-term solutions to improve lives in poorer countries and build safer communities.
- Works in over 130 countries, focusing on places where poverty, hunger and emergencies are of most concern, e.g. Africa and Asia.
- Ireland's ODA impact 2024 (Figure 27.12): total ODA was €2.35 billion; supported people in over 100 countries; over 8 million people directly supported through partnership with Irish NGOs.
- Partners: local charities, global organisations like the UN and research teams in Ireland and abroad.
- Emergency aid: managed by the Department of Foreign Affairs and funded by Irish taxpayers. Irish Aid is Ireland's largest bilateral aid programme. Ireland is renowned for being fair, caring and responsible.
- Long-term aid: goes beyond crises; helps communities recover and become less reliant on aid, e.g. funding education and training for young people and educating teachers and local leaders to continue programmes after Irish Aid leaves. Empowers communities to lead change.

PRINCIPLES OF ODA PROGRAMMES
1. Partnership approach: cooperates with partner governments, local communities, UN agencies, NGOs and the private sector so aid fits local needs and is managed locally.
2. 'A Better World' policy: Ireland's official international development policy; aims for a more just, equal and sustainable world, with a primary focus on 'reaching the furthest behind first' and tackling humanitarian, environmental and governance challenges at their root.
3. Local engagement: works closely with local groups, e.g. in Ethiopia supporting small dairy farmers to improve methods and output, so help matches real local needs.
4. Global cooperation: supports the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and teamwork to tackle poverty and climate change.
5. Support for civil society: funds local and international organisations, empowering communities, promoting fair leadership and supporting people in emergencies.
- Irish Aid is admired internationally for being high quality, creative and based on partnership with local partners.

CASE STUDY: IRISH AID IN ETHIOPIA
- Ethiopia lies in the Sahel region on the southern edge of the Sahara Desert.
- Climate change has caused drought, desertification, famine and population displacement.
- Irish Aid has partnered with Ethiopian communities, charities and experts since 1994, using sustainable, locally owned solutions.
- Five key areas: gender equality, governance, food, social protection, humanitarian action.
- Ethiopia was the top recipient of Irish bilateral ODA in 2024.
1. Gender equality
- Women supported to set up small businesses with training, access to credit and livestock, giving skills, confidence, income, household security and independence.
- Investing in women-led enterprises promotes economic empowerment and gender equality (links to SDG 5).
- In the Afar region, Irish Aid supports an initiative to tackle Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) and child marriage.
2. Governance
- Strong governance and local ownership: works with communities, charities, health workers, researchers and farmers.
- Supports farmer education programmes and cooperatives so projects respond to local needs and communities take part in decisions.
- Funds the Civil Society Support Programme, which contributes to development, poverty reduction and good governance; communities identify their own needs and propose improvements.
3. Food security
- Supports Ethiopian researchers and farmers to grow more food in difficult climates.
- Drought-resistant crops such as potatoes; sustainable methods like agroforestry (trees and shrubs planted alongside crops to protect soil and keep moisture).
- In Tigray: water storage tanks, irrigation channels and small dams capture rainfall for droughts; some farmers increased harvests by up to 30% even in low rainfall.
4. Social protection
- Heavy investment in health, nutrition and education: training local nurses and midwives, improving clinics, nutrition for mothers and babies.
- More births with skilled midwives and higher infant vaccination rates. Between 2020 and 2025 births with a midwife present rose from 18% to 28%; infant mortality fell.
- School feeding programmes and clinics that check children for malnutrition; well-fed children have energy to attend school and learn, and early treatment saves lives.
5. Humanitarian action
- In drought, crop failure and conflict, Irish Aid responds quickly with food, seeds, household items and financial aid to restart livelihoods.
- Cash assistance lets people buy essentials while supporting local markets.
- In 2024 Ireland spent over €40 million on food, health, education and peacebuilding in Ethiopia, through programmes reaching more than 61,000 people. (Summary also notes 5,000+ families received emergency food/support.)
Conclusion
- A strong example of modern, effective development cooperation: blends humanitarian aid with long-term development, local ownership and evidence-based strategies.
- Shows how targeted, sustained support empowers communities, builds climate resilience and creates a path out of poverty.

TOP 10 RECIPIENTS OF IRISH BILATERAL ODA 2024 (FIGURE 27.18, OECD; € thousands)
- Ethiopia 40,891; Ukraine 33,887; Occupied Palestinian Territory 30,460; Mozambique 26,074; Tanzania 25,988; Malawi 24,959; Uganda 21,466; Sierra Leone 19,004; South Sudan 14,484; Sudan 11,440.
- Ukraine and the Occupied Palestinian Territory are the top-ten recipients not in Africa.
- Difference between Ethiopia and Sudan: about €29.5 million.

EXAM SKILLS (from the chapter's sample answers)
- 'Name one country Ireland gave humanitarian assistance to after a crisis and state one cause; discuss how assistance was used': Sudan, civil war; use €14m + €2.5m, NGOs GOAL/Trócaire/Concern, 50 tonnes of supplies to South Sudan, Zamzam camp, UN advocacy.
- 'Discuss how Irish Aid impacts one Global South country': Ethiopia; social protection (18% to 28% midwife births), food security (potatoes, agroforestry, Tigray up to 30%), gender equality (women's businesses, Afar FGM and child marriage initiative).
